title: Should, ought to and had better

sections.title: Should and ought to: obligations, recommendations and probability
sections.content:
We can often use either should or ought to to talk about obligations and recommendations (e.g. You should / ought to finish your homework before you go out) and probability (e.g. It should / ought to be ready by now) although in general should is used more frequently. Ought to is used particularly in speech and most often to talk about obligation rather than probability.
When we conclude, on the basis of some evidence we have, that something is certain or very likely we can use must (see Unit 18) but not should / ought to:
• It's the third time she's been skating this week. She must really enjoy it.
Note also the following details –
☆ we prefer should when we say what an outside authority recommends:
• The manual says that the computer should be disconnected from the power supply before the cover is removed. (rather than … ought to be disconnected …)
☆ we use should (or would), not ought to, when we give advice with I …:
• I should leave early tomorrow, if I were you. (or I'd leave …; or I'd leave …)
☆ we prefer should in questions, particularly wh-questions:
• What should I do if I have any problems?     Should I ring you at home?

sections.title: Should/ought to have + past participle: regret and expectation
sections.content:
We use should / ought to + have + past participle to talk about something that didn't happen in the past and we are sorry that it didn't:
• We should / ought to have waited for the rain to stop. (I'm sorry we didn't)
We often use this pattern to indicate some regret or criticism and the negative forms shouldn't / oughtn't to have are almost always used in this way.
We also use should / ought to + have + past participle to talk about an expectation that something happened, has happened, or will happen:
• If the flight was on time, he should / ought to have arrived in Jakarta early this morning.

sections.title: Should in offers, confirmations and shall
sections.content:
We can use should in questions that are offers or that request confirmation or advice:
• Should I phone for a taxi for you?
• Who should I pass the message to?
Note that in sentences like these we can also use shall with a very similar meaning. There are two uses of shall in formal style that are distinct from should: 'I shall' means 'I intend to' and 'I should' means 'I ought to':
• I shall read the script on the train tomorrow. (or I'll read …) and
• I should read the script on the train tomorrow but I know that I'll be too tired.

sections.title: Had better: urgent advice, demands and threats
sections.content:
We can use had better instead of should / ought to, especially in spoken English, to say that we think it is a good idea to do something:
• If you're not well, you'd better ask Clare to go instead. (or … you should / ought to …)
although we don't use it to talk about the past or to make general comments:
• You should / ought to have caught a later train. (not You had better have caught …)
• I don't think parents should / ought to give children sweets. (not … parents had better give …)
We prefer had better if we want to express particular urgency or in demands and threats:
• There's someone moving about downstairs. We'd better call the police, quickly.
Note that the negative form is had better not, and in questions the subject comes after had:
• He'd better not be late again or he'll be in trouble.
• Had we better get a taxi? (or Should we get …?)

exercises.question: Thomas is running so well at the moment that he ___ the 800 metres easily.
exercises.hint: Probability about a future event → should/ought to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should/ought to win
Probability about a future event → should/ought to + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: Where ___ the cheese? In the fridge?
exercises.hint: Question asking for advice → should preferred.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should I put (question — should preferred)
Question asking for advice → should preferred.

exercises.question: The tickets ___ a couple of weeks before we go on holiday.
options: Both should be sent and ought to be sent
exercises.hint: Both should and ought to work for passive obligation.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both should be sent and ought to be sent
Both should and ought to work for passive obligation. Choose the passive form that matches the tense and aspect of the active version.

exercises.question: All packaging ___ before switching on the printer for the first time.
options: should be removed (instruction from authority → should preferred)
exercises.hint: Instruction from authority (manual) → should preferred.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should be removed (instruction from authority → should preferred)
Instruction from authority (manual) → should preferred.

exercises.question: It's important to look smart at the interview. You ___ a suit.
exercises.hint: Personal recommendation → should/ought to + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should wear / ought to wear (recommendation)
Personal recommendation → should/ought to + infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: There are many people who think the President ___ years ago.
options: should have resigned / ought to have resigned (past regret)
exercises.hint: Past event that didn't happen + regret → should have / ought to have + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should have resigned / ought to have resigned (past regret)
Past event that didn't happen + regret → should have / ought to have + past participle. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: If you want my advice, I ___ by train rather than car.
options: should go (advice with 'I' → should, not ought to)
exercises.hint: Giving advice with 'I...' → should (not ought to).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should go (advice with 'I' → should, not ought to)
Giving advice with 'I...' → should (not ought to).

exercises.question: I can't imagine what's happened to Vita. She ___ here by now.
options: should have arrived / ought to have arrived (expectation not met)
exercises.hint: Expectation that something has already happened → should/ought to have + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should have arrived / ought to have arrived (expectation not met)
Expectation that something has already happened → should/ought to have + past participle. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: A timetable ___ be set for withdrawing the army.
exercises.hint: Both should (recommendation) and must (obligation/necessity) are possible here.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should/must (both possible — obligation)
Both should (recommendation) and must (obligation/necessity) are possible here.

exercises.question: Lev isn't home yet. He ___ have been held up at work.
exercises.hint: Drawing a strong conclusion based on evidence → must (not should/ought to).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must (strong conclusion based on evidence)
Drawing a strong conclusion based on evidence → must (not should/ought to).

exercises.question: He went to school with my mother, so he ___ be well over 50.
exercises.hint: Very certain logical deduction → must (not should).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must (logical deduction — very certain)
Very certain logical deduction → must (not should).

exercises.question: If you smell gas, you ___ phone the emergency number.
exercises.hint: Urgent safety warning → must.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must (urgent warning)
Urgent safety warning → must. Urgent safety warning → must — check the sentence for the grammatical signal that requires this specific form.

exercises.question: You ___ try to visit Nepal – it's a beautiful country.
exercises.hint: Personal recommendation — both should and must are acceptable.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should/must (recommendation — both possible)
Personal recommendation — both should and must are acceptable.

exercises.question: A: There's something wrong with David's computer yet again. B: He should wish he'd never bought it. → Correction?
options: should have never bought it (past regret)
Both are correct if meaning is past regret
exercises.hint: Past regret → shouldn't have bought it (negative, no 'never' before bought).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: shouldn't have bought it
Ever in questions about experience signals the present perfect. It means "at any time in your life up to now". The question is not about a specific occasion but about whether the experience has happened at any point.

exercises.question: B: 'Yes. I shall do more exercise, but I never seem to have time.' → Correction?
options: I should/had better/ought to do more exercise (obligation, not future plan)
exercises.hint: 'I shall' here implies intention but context is obligation/regret → should/ought to/had better.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I should/had better/ought to do more exercise (obligation, not future plan)
'I shall' here implies intention but context is obligation/regret → should/ought to/had better. The present simple is correct here. Check the context: is this a permanent fact, a habitual action, a performative declaration, or a stative verb describing a state? All of these take the present simple rather than the continuous.

exercises.question: B: 'You'd better have worn a thicker coat.' → Correction?
options: should have worn / ought to have worn (past, not had better)
exercises.hint: Talking about the past → should have worn / ought to have worn (had better can't be used for past).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should have worn / ought to have worn (past, not had better)
Talking about the past → should have worn / ought to have worn (had better can't be used for past).

exercises.sentence: You should to take more exercise — the doctor said so.
exercises.correction: You should take more exercise — the doctor said so.
exercises.hint: 'Should' is a modal — bare infinitive follows, no 'to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: You should take more exercise
'Should' is a modal verb followed by the bare infinitive. 'Should to take' is a very common learner error. All modals (should, would, could, might, must, shall, will) are followed directly by the base form of the verb.

exercises.sentence: We had better to leave now or we'll miss the train.
exercises.correction: We had better leave now or we'll miss the train.
exercises.hint: 'Had better' is always followed by the bare infinitive — no 'to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: We had better leave
'Had better + bare infinitive' is a fixed expression. Unlike 'ought to' and 'have to', it never uses 'to' before the verb. 'Had better to leave' is always wrong. Note: 'had better' is negative: 'had better not leave'.

exercises.sentence: You ought leave earlier if you want to avoid the rush hour.
exercises.correction: You ought to leave earlier if you want to avoid the rush hour.
exercises.hint: 'Ought to' — unlike other modals — requires 'to' before the infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: You ought to leave earlier
'Ought to' is unique among modals: it requires 'to' before the bare infinitive. 'Ought leave' is always wrong. Compare: 'should leave' (no to) vs 'ought to leave' (with to). Both express advice/obligation but 'ought to' is slightly more formal.

exercises.prompt: Make a sentence using 'had better' as a warning:
exercises.hint: Subject + had better + bare infinitive + or + consequence
exercises.explanation:
Answer: You had better apologise or you'll regret it
'Had better + bare infinitive' expresses a strong recommendation or warning. 'Or' introduces the negative consequence if the advice is ignored. Note: never use 'to' after 'had better'.
